summary:
Central Visayas, the region of the central Philippine islands governed from the Cebu area, stands under the national framework of the Republic of the Philippines. National law does not criminalise same-sex relations or transgender identity, and there is no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity; the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending in Congress for 25 years. Protections that do exist are sub-national, and the region contains an unusually active concentration of them at the provincial and municipal level.

Mandaue City, in metropolitan Cebu, adopted the implementing rules and regulations of its Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024 in a signing jointly conducted with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and UNDP Philippines. The instrument is operational rather than declaratory: it sets out how the ordinance is to be applied, and a visitor subjected to SOGIE-based discrimination in Mandaue can invoke a functioning local ordinance with a designated federation partner. In the municipality of Carmen in northern Cebu, the Sangguniang Bayan approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance on SOGI grounds by unanimous vote in June 2025, days before the close of Pride Month.

The 2026 travel-risk assessment that scores Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers at 69 of 100 but places trans travellers lower at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band, describes the capital rather than Central Visayas; no equivalent scoring for the Cebu metropolitan area is sourced here.
tangentialFactors:
The protections in Central Visayas belong to the wider Philippine pattern of local ordinance coverage in the absence of a national statute: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances have been adopted across eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities nationwide. The region's cluster is notable for being operationalised rather than merely passed, with Mandaue's implementing rules signed jointly with the mayor and a LGBT federation under UN development-programme support.

Sectoral national protections, which reach into the region regardless of local ordinance coverage, include the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (SOGIE harassment carries a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty) and the Safe Spaces Act and Magna Carta of Women (slurs and ridicule attract fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar). The Code of Professional Responsibility, updated in 2023, bars lawyers from discriminating against clients on SOGIE grounds. The armed forces have permitted openly transgender personnel since 2017, with uniform policy following the birth-certificate gender marker.
localsOnly:
For residents of Cebu province, Mandaue and Carmen, the operative layer of protection is local ordinance backed by a municipality or city administration, and the practical route is complaint through the LGU's designated mechanism rather than through a national agency, since no national SOGIE equality statute exists. Carmen's ordinance was adopted unanimously, which gives it stable footing against later political reversal at the municipal level.

Legal gender recognition remains unavailable to Central Visayas residents as it is to all Filipinos: the Clerical Error Law forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court's 2008 holding in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan denies legal gender change even after gender-affirming surgery. The pending recognition bill has not been enacted.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source article reporting the northern Cebu ordinance does not identify the municipality or the exact date of passage. The identification as Carmen, by unanimous vote in June 2025, rests on other sourcing and is stated here as such; the underlying article carries only the fact of a municipal Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance passed days before the close of Pride Month, within Central Visayas.

No trans-specific killings, assaults or institutional-hostility incidents in Central Visayas are documented within the 2024-2025 national violence series reviewed for this record. This is an absence in the sourced material rather than a finding that no such incidents occurred; the national pattern documented elsewhere in the Philippines includes trans women killed in June 2025 and earlier. The region's national screening, detention and document rules are the ones described in the national framework and are not independently sourced here for Central Visayas facilities.
